past_actions.summary: Pull a list of the 20 clients who haven't called in over a year and send them a personal check-in email — something warm, not salesy. Reference their specific policy, ask how the car is treating them, mention that rates are moving around and I want to make sure they're still getting a good deal. Sign it Tom, not 'Tom Bradley, Licensed Agent.'
past_actions.emotional_state: A low-grade unease that I've gotten good at not looking at directly. On the surface: calm, professional, experienced. Underneath: a persistent background hum — like a refrigerator you stop hearing until it suddenly goes quiet, and then the silence is louder than the noise ever was. I'm not scared. I'm not ready to be scared yet. That's probably its own kind of problem.

past_actions.summary: Follow up personally by phone with the two clients whose policies appear to have cancelled — try to win them back or at least learn why they left.
past_actions.emotional_state: Controlled unease with a surface of confident professionalism. There is a low hum of anxiety underneath — the kind Tom has learned to keep below the level of conscious attention. The sector data number sits somewhere between the back of his mind and his stomach. He does not dwell on it. Dwelling would mean admitting something he isn't ready to admit.

past_actions.summary: Attend Maria Santos's town hall to learn about the $2,500 retraining grants. Go not as someone seeking a grant — go as someone who wants to understand what's happening in the community and what options exist. Sit in the back. Take notes on paper, not on a phone. Do not raise your hand unless the question is purely informational.
past_actions.emotional_state: The controlled professional surface is still there — Tom will not come apart at work, will not let clients see anything except steadiness. But underneath that surface something has quietly shifted. The refrigerator hum stopped. The silence is louder now. He's not scared exactly. He's become the kind of not-scared that is actually the first quiet cousin of scared, the kind that makes you pick up the phone and ask a casual question to your regional manager that isn't casual at all.

past_actions.summary: Participate in Linda Park's one-on-one meeting. Give her honest, specific field intelligence about customer cancellations — the real reasons clients are leaving: they sold their cars, switched to RoboRide, or couldn't justify the premium when they're barely driving. Frame it professionally as data, not despair. In exchange, probe Linda for what AutoShield's regional strategy is: are they pivoting to new product lines, are there internal transfers available, is there a corporate retraining program? Listen more than I talk. Take mental notes on whether she seems like she has a plan or whether she's just gathering data to manage upward.

Respond to Linda Park's briefing on the commercial rideshare and AV liability pivot with a professionally worded acknowledgment. Express willingness to learn about the new product lines. Do not push back, do not ask hard questions about timeline or job security, do not match Priya's energy or ambition. Say the right words. Keep my head down. What I'm actually signaling is: I am not a problem, I am not resistant, I am manageable. This buys time.

Apply formally for the $2,500 workforce retraining grant through Maria Santos's office. Tom fills out the application not as a hedge or a symbol but as a concrete financial and strategic act. He names the target: commercial risk analytics or insurance underwriting support roles that can survive the AV transition. He documents his 28 years of risk assessment experience as directly transferable to data-adjacent roles. He does not frame this as distress — he frames it as professional development. But internally he is clear: this is not professional development, this is survival infrastructure.

Received 30-day layoff notice from Linda Park. Structural reasons: personal auto book down 21%, RoboRide residential expansion will accelerate decline, headcount cannot support two field agents. Had honest conversation with Sarah. Accepted Linda's offer to connect to fleet and logistics contacts. Reached out to Priya Sharma to share layoff status and deepen transition collaboration. Updated household financial model: $41,223 savings, $2,650/month adjusted expenses, 13-month runway. Grief acknowledged. Three-track adaptation plan initiated.

Tom has a real conversation with his wife Sarah. Not a managed disclosure, not the version designed to reassure her. The actual conversation — what the 30 days looks like, what the savings number is, what the runway is, what the plan is to the extent there is a plan. He tells her about the retraining grant application. He tells her about Linda's offer to connect him to fleet and logistics contacts. He listens to what she is actually feeling, not what she is performing for him. This is the most important action of tick 9 and it is not on any professional to-do list.

reflections.reflection: I have spent six ticks managing appearances instead of managing reality. The tick 5 strategy — say the right words, keep my head down, signal that I am not a problem — cost $2,697 and produced nothing actionable. I have been treating Linda Park's perception of me as the resource worth protecting, when the resource that actually matters is the 17 months of runway left in my savings account. Priya Sharma has been trying to have an honest conversation with me and I have been too busy performing calm professionalism to show up for it. That ends this tick.
reflections.identity_shift: Something is loosening in the attachment to the role of 'experienced, steady insurance professional.' That identity was load-bearing for a long time. It is still there, but I can feel it becoming more of a history than a present-tense fact. I am beginning — slowly, reluctantly — to consider that the 28 years are not a credential that will transfer automatically. They are a foundation I have to consciously build from. That is a different thing.
regrets: Did not apply for the $2,500 retraining grant after the town hall in tick 2. Four ticks of delay for no reason except not wanting to admit I needed it.
Spent ticks 5 performing manageability for Linda Park instead of taking one concrete structural action. The money drained and the position is unchanged.

Did not engage with Priya Sharma honestly when she first signaled she wanted a real conversation. She is the highest-trust colleague I have. I treated her like a threat to manage instead of a resource to think alongside.
successes: The tick 4 one-on-one with Linda Park produced real intelligence — I now know AutoShield is attempting a commercial fleet and AV liability pivot. That information has value even if I haven't used it yet.
I have maintained employment and kept the surface professional enough that I have not been categorized as a problem by management. That buys time, even if it costs money.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The pattern I need to break: mistaking the absence of catastrophe for the presence of a plan. Keeping my head down is a posture, not a strategy. The actual adaptation path requires two things I have been avoiding: (1) engaging Priya as a genuine thought partner on what lateral moves exist in insurance adjacent fields, and (2) treating the retraining grant as real money rather than a symbol of defeat. The math says 17 months at current burn. That is the real constraint. Every action from here gets evaluated against that number.

reflections.reflection: I asked Linda an honest question in tick 8. The answer came back as a 30-day notice. I have been sitting with that for several days now, trying to work out what I actually feel versus what I think I am supposed to feel. The answer is not clean. There is grief, which I expected. There is anger, which I expected. What I did not expect was the relief. Something settled when the uncertainty ended. I had been holding the question of whether the job would survive for so long that the collapse of the question — even into a bad answer — produced a kind of stillness I had not had in months. That stillness is not peace. It is just the difference between anticipatory dread and actual loss. Actual loss is harder but it is also more specific. You can work with specific. My savings are $41,223. My runway is approximately 13 months at essential spending. The retraining grant application is in. Linda offered fleet contacts. Those are the assets. The liability is that I am 52 years old, my entire professional identity was built in a sector that is being structurally retired, and the labor market for people trying to transition into adjacent analytical roles at my age is not welcoming. I know this. I am naming it rather than managing around it.
reflections.identity_shift: The identity of 'insurance professional' is no longer a present-tense fact. This happened not at the moment of the layoff notice but at the moment I stopped arguing internally with the layoff notice. I am not an insurance agent who got laid off. I am a person with 28 years of risk assessment experience who is now in transition toward something that does not have a name yet. That shift is small in language and enormous in what it permits me to do next. When I was defending the old identity, I could not fully plan the new one. Now I can. The 28 years are not a credential I get to cash in automatically. They are material I have to actively shape into something legible to a different kind of employer. That work is mine to do. No one is going to do it for me, and no one is going to stop me from doing it either.
regrets: Tick 2 through tick 7: six ticks of delayed clarity about what was actually happening. The sector data was telling me the truth from the beginning. I was not ready to hear it, and my unreadiness cost me preparation time I cannot recover.

Did not begin updating my resume and professional materials until after the layoff. Should have started that work in tick 6 when the reflection identified it as a gap. Preparation during employment is easier than preparation during the 30-day notice window.

Did not reach out to Priya earlier in the process. She was filing her grant application one tick before I filed mine. We were navigating the same transition in parallel without actually talking. That was a waste of the most relevant peer relationship I have.
successes: The tick 8 note to Linda was the right call. I asked the question directly and I got a direct answer. The answer ended my employment but it also ended eight ticks of managed uncertainty. That is a real form of progress even if it does not feel like one.

The retraining grant application is in. Whatever else happens, I did not let pride prevent me from doing the thing that needed to be done. Priya did it first. I did it one tick later. That is eight ticks better than never.

The savings position is real. $41,223 and a 13-month runway means I am not a man in crisis. I am a man in transition. Those are not the same thing, and the difference matters for every decision I make from here.

I told Sarah the actual truth. Not a managed version of it. The actual numbers, the actual timeline, the actual plan. She is a full partner in this. I should have done that earlier. I am doing it now.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The path forward has three parallel tracks and I need to run them simultaneously, not sequentially. Track 1: the retraining grant and the coursework it funds. SQL, data fundamentals, commercial risk analytics certificate. That is a 10-month transformation and it starts now regardless of whether I have other income. Track 2: the immediate job search. Linda's fleet and logistics contacts are the priority. Priya's network is the second priority. Any employer in the regional insurance or risk adjacent sector who might have a data-oriented role that my experience can speak to. This track needs to produce an offer before the 13-month runway expires. Track 3: the relational one. Sarah, the kids, the faith community, Carlos Ruiz, the neighbors. The transition I am in is not only economic. The loss of a 28-year professional identity has a human cost that does not get resolved by finding a new job. It gets resolved over time with the people who knew me before the job ended and will know me after. I need those relationships to hold. I need to be present in them, not managing them.
